newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks seen down on finance sector shake-up.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks seen down on finance sector shake-up.

text.p: Thai stocks are expected to fall this week with a period of short covering by foreigners set to end and a finance sector shakedown due to hit, traders and analysts said.
The country's stock index closed last week at 528.18, up a hefty 10 percent over the week. Foreign buying to cover short positions gave the market a boost.
But traders say uncertainty over new Bank of Thailand measures announced on Friday to support the ailing finance sector could spark selling.

The measures will force 16 weak finance companies to merge with healthy ones. The action was broadly welcomed but concerns surround the implementation of the central bank's plans and the possibility that unprotected foreign creditors and shareholders of the firms will face losses.

Traders said those fears could spark further sales in a battered sector which continues to face falling revenues, declining asset quality and high funding costs amid Thailand's worst economic slump in over a decade.

"I think basically we're looking at retail selling next week. Retail investors' stocks in the 16 finance companies may never list again, and that could cause some concern around the rest of the finance sector," said the chief of sales chief at a large European broker.
The Thai bourse has lost 36.5 percent of its value so far this year and the stock index has recently been lingering near eight-year lows.

Although a foreign-led technical rally could continue on Monday, aided by some end-of-quarter window dressing, last week's gains are unlikely to be repeated as foreign houses have now covered most of their short positions, traders said.
They said funds from Hong Kong, Taiwan and the United States were responsible for the brief market rally last week.

"We've been doing some covering out of New York but I think most should be over by now. The custodian banks seem to have a June 30 agenda, and basically by then I think everybody should have covered everything," the trader said.
Currency controls introduced in May to close off baht funds to currency speculators continued to take a toll and near-term corporate liquidity remained a serious concern, analysts said.

"My sense is that a lot of major corporates are dead concerned about tight liquidity. June 30 is a major payment date and I think there are going to be a lot of bills that are not going to be paid," said Russell Kopp, head of research at Kleinwort Benson.

Weak economic data released on Thursday and the government's downward revision of growth forecasts during a budget debate last week pointed to continued shakiness in economic fundamentals which should deter most long-term investors, analysts said.
Bearish market predictions have it that the stock index will bottom at under 400 in the next two months, analysts said.

Volumes which rose to around six billion baht ($250 million) a day last week will likely fall with the closure of the market for a half-year holiday on Tuesday and the Hong Kong market's holiday for the territory's handover to China.
